Single-cell DeCovarT inference: profile information, intervals and the REML calibration

Bastien Chassagnol

2026-10-28

Source: vignettes/theory-single-cell-inference.qmd

Scope

This vignette derives the intervals and tests for the single-cell mixture fitted by deconvolute_single_cell(): one bulk sample, one single-cell reference, a composition on the simplex and two technical scales estimated with it. The model, the closed-form scales and the profile Newton fit are in the single-cell generative and optimisation vignette. The population-level counterpart, with the regularity conditions, the three first-order tests and the boundary theory that this vignette reuses, is the population inference vignette.

  1. Sec. 1 states the model and its scale equivariance.
  2. Sec. 2 gives the information matrix and the Schur complement that carries the cost of estimating the scales.
  3. Sec. 3 states the limit that justifies a first-order interval for one bulk sample.
  4. Sec. 4 derives the six interval methods of confint_single_cell(), and Sec. 4.1 the calibration for few genes.
  5. Sec. 5 gives the intervals for the scales, Sec. 6 the likelihood-ratio tests and the boundary, and Sec. 7 what none of these intervals covers.

Model and scale equivariance

For bulk sample i with n_i cells and capture ratio a_i, the averaged mixture of independent cells is

\boldsymbol{y}\mid\boldsymbol{p} \sim\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p},\;\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr), \qquad \boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}, \qquad c=a_in_i,\quad\phi=a_i^{2}n_i, \tag{1}

with \tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} the mean of a type-j cell on raw counts and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} its within-type covariance. The composition is charted by \boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\rho}) with a Helmert basis \mathbf{V} (ILR chart). Concentrating the scales out gives the profile log-likelihood

\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho}) =-\frac{G}{2}\log Q(\boldsymbol{p}) -\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})+\text{const}, \qquad Q(\boldsymbol{p})=\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}, \tag{2}

with \hat{\boldsymbol{r}}=\boldsymbol{y}-\hat c(\boldsymbol{p})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p} the generalised least-squares residual (closed-form scales).

Scale equivariance. Multiply the bulk by k>0. The closed forms give \hat c(k\boldsymbol{y})=k\hat c(\boldsymbol{y}), \hat{\boldsymbol{r}} scales by k, Q by k^{2} and \hat\phi by k^{2}, so

\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho};k\boldsymbol{y})=\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho};\boldsymbol{y})-G\log k . \tag{3}

The shift does not depend on \boldsymbol{\rho}. The estimate \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}, the profile Hessian, every interval built from them and every likelihood ratio are unchanged, while (\hat c,\hat\phi) move to (k\hat c,k^{2}\hat\phi). The capture ratio and the number of cells enter only through c and \phi. A fixed capture ratio is therefore a relabelling of the scales and cannot change the composition, which is why a simulation study need not cross it with the other factors.

Information and the Schur complement

Write \boldsymbol{\eta}=(c,\phi), \boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1} and \boldsymbol{m}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p}. The expected information of Eq. 1 has the blocks

I_{c\phi}=0,\qquad I_{\phi\phi}=\frac{G}{2\phi^{2}},\qquad I_{cc}=\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}}{\phi},\qquad I_{p_jc}=\frac{c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}}{\phi},\qquad I_{p_j\phi}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j})}{2\phi}. \tag{4}

The two scales are orthogonal to each other, but neither is orthogonal to the composition. The asymptotic covariance of \hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}} is therefore the inverse of the Schur complement

I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\mid\boldsymbol{\eta}} =I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\rho}} -I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\eta}}I_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\eta}}^{-1}I_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\rho}}, \tag{5}

which is never larger than I_{\boldsymbol{\rho}\boldsymbol{\rho}}: estimating the scales widens the composition intervals, and the Schur complement accounts for it without a separate correction. When an interest parameter is orthogonal to the nuisance, its standard error is the same whether the nuisance is known or estimated (Cox and Reid 1987); Eq. 4 shows that this does not happen here. A scalar interest parameter can always be made orthogonal by reparametrisation; a vector one in general cannot.

The fit uses the observed counterpart. By the envelope theorem the negative Hessian of the profile log-likelihood Eq. 2 is the Schur complement of the observed information at the closed-form scales (profile Hessian), so profile-based and joint Wald intervals coincide. vcov_single_cell() and the fit return

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=\bigl(-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\bigr)^{-1}, \qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) =\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}\,\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\,\mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}}^{\top}, \tag{6}

as vcov_rho and vcov, with \mathbf{J}_{\boldsymbol{\psi}} the ILR Jacobian. The complementary Schur complement, which removes \boldsymbol{\rho} from the scale block, gives vcov_nuisance for (c,\phi).

Small-dispersion asymptotics in the number of cells

One bulk sample has no replicate, so the usual limit in the number of independent observations does not apply, and the G genes are not independent replicates either. Divide the bulk by c: the per-cell bulk \tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}=\boldsymbol{y}/c satisfies

\tilde{\boldsymbol{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}_G\bigl(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{p},\;n^{-1}\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr), \qquad n=c^{2}/\phi, \tag{7}

a family whose dispersion 1/n shrinks as the number of cells grows. That is the small-dispersion limit of Jørgensen (1987). Under it the maximum-likelihood estimate is asymptotically normal around the realised composition, with covariance the inverse of Eq. 5, and the likelihood-ratio statistic is asymptotically \chi^{2}. The approximation improves with the number of cells of every type, m_j=np_j, not with G. The number of genes enters through the residual degrees of freedom of the covariance scale (Sec. 4.1). With Gaussian cells the sum is exactly Gaussian at any n; with counts, Eq. 7 is a central-limit approximation that needs every m_j to be large.

Intervals for the composition

confint_single_cell() takes the bulk and the reference moments, refits, and returns one of six intervals. Its estimate is the composition that the likelihood optimises, before any conversion between cell and transcript fractions.

Delta method. The "wald" interval uses the diagonal of Eq. 6. It is symmetric and can leave [0,1] for a rare type.

Inverse ILR chart. The "ilr" interval forms the Wald interval in \boldsymbol{\rho} and maps it back. For J=2 the endpoints of the single coordinate are mapped by \boldsymbol{\psi}. For J>2, draws \boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}},\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\rho}})\bigr), b=1,\ldots,n_draws, are mapped to \boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{\rho}^{(b)}) and the interval is the marginal quantile of each proportion. Every draw is a composition, so the interval stays inside the simplex. Pass seed for a reproducible Monte Carlo map.

Profile likelihood. The "profile" interval (confint_profile_single_cell()) fixes p_j at a trial value, refits the other proportions and both scales with restricted_mle_single_cell(), and keeps the values whose deviance stays below the \chi^{2}_{1} quantile (Wilks 1938). It does not depend on the chart and stays in [0,1]. An endpoint that lands on a face is not a Wilks interval and must be read with the boundary test of Sec. 6.

Firth penalty. The "firth" interval maximises \ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})+\tfrac12\log\det\{-\nabla^{2}\ell^{\ast}(\boldsymbol{\rho})\} (fit_firth_single_cell()) (Firth 1993), then reports the Wald interval at the penalised estimate. The penalty uses the observed profile information, with the scales concentrated out, so it adds no free scale. The information in \boldsymbol{\rho} inherits the factor \mathbf{S}(\boldsymbol{p}) of the ILR Jacobian, whose determinant vanishes at a face, so the penalty tends to -\infty there and the penalised estimate is always interior. Firth’s exact removal of the first-order bias holds for the canonical parameter of an exponential family; this curved Gaussian family needs a simulation check (Firth penalisation).

Parametric bootstrap. The "bootstrap" interval (bootstrap_single_cell()) draws \boldsymbol{Y}^{(b)}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\hat c\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}},\hat\phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})\bigr), refits the profile model, and returns percentile intervals for the composition and for both scales (Efron 1979). The reference moments stay fixed.

Reference bootstrap. The "reference" interval (reference_bootstrap_single_cell()) propagates the uncertainty of the reference itself. When every type has at least two donors it resamples donors within each type, rebuilds (\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}) and refits the observed bulk. With one donor it resamples cells within each type and regenerates the bulk from the fitted model with the original moments, then refits with the resampled moments. Drawing that bulk from the resampled moments instead would hide the reference error, since the bulk and the reference would then agree by construction. Shuffling cell-type labels is not an interval: the fitted composition moves with the labels, which is equivariance, not sampling variability.

Few genes: the REML calibration

The covariance scale is estimated from the whitened residual, \hat\phi=Q(\hat{\boldsymbol{p}})/G, after fitting J mean parameters (J-1 coordinates of \boldsymbol{\rho} and c). It has \nu=G-J residual degrees of freedom, and the maximum-likelihood divisor G biases it downwards by a factor of about \nu/G. Every interval that plugs in \hat\phi is then too narrow when G is small: with G=20 and J=4, \nu/G=0.8.

variance = "reml" in confint_single_cell() and confint_profile_single_cell() corrects for those degrees of freedom, as restricted maximum likelihood does for a variance component:

  • the covariances of Eq. 6 are inflated by G/\nu;
  • Wald and ILR quantiles come from t_{\nu} instead of the normal, with a multivariate t for the Monte Carlo ILR map when J>2;
  • \phi gets the chi-square interval \bigl[G\hat\phi/\chi^{2}_{\nu;1-\alpha/2},\;G\hat\phi/\chi^{2}_{\nu;\alpha/2}\bigr];
  • the profile interval uses the cut-off

D_{\alpha}=G\log\Bigl(1+\frac{F_{1,\nu;1-\alpha}}{\nu}\Bigr), \tag{8}

in place of \chi^{2}_{1;1-\alpha}.

Eq. 8 is exact in a linear model with an unknown variance: with the variance profiled out, twice the log likelihood ratio for one linear constraint equals G\log(1+F/\nu) for an F_{1,\nu} statistic. As \nu\to\infty it tends to \chi^{2}_{1}. The bootstrap methods ignore variance, because they draw \hat\phi afresh in every replicate. The Monte Carlo check of these calibrations is scripts/benchmark_metrics/check_confidence_interval_coverage.R: the maximum-likelihood intervals under-cover with G=10 genes, and the REML calibration brings them back to the nominal level.

Intervals for the two scales

confint_single_cell() also returns nuisance, intervals for c and \phi. The default nuisance$interval is a Wald interval on (\log c,\log\phi) from the complementary Schur complement, which removes \boldsymbol{\rho}, mapped back by the exponential, so both limits are positive. nuisance$interval_wald is the symmetric normal interval on (c,\phi) itself. Under variance = "reml", \phi gets the chi-square interval of Sec. 4.1. The bootstrap methods replace both with percentile intervals.

I_{c\phi}=0 does not reduce this block to two one-parameter problems: the complement still accounts for the estimation of the composition. The derived quantities \hat a=\hat\phi/\hat c and \hat n=\hat c^{2}/\hat\phi inherit the downward bias of \hat\phi, so \hat n is biased upwards. They describe the sample; \hat n is a number of cells only when the capture ratio is known, from the same platform or from paired samples (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021).

Likelihood-ratio tests and the boundary

lrt_single_cell() tests a value of the composition with the scales profiled out under both hypotheses. An interior null, p_j=c_0\in(0,1), is calibrated by \chi^{2} with as many degrees of freedom as constraints. A null on a face, p_j=0, puts the true parameter on the boundary of the simplex: the limit is the projection of a Gaussian score on the tangent cone, and for one absent type with orthogonal information the statistic follows \tfrac12\chi^{2}_{0}+\tfrac12\chi^{2}_{1} (Chernoff 1954; Self and Liang 1987). lrt_single_cell() counts the null proportions on the boundary and switches to the chi-bar-square calibration automatically. The restricted fit on a face, restricted_mle_single_cell(), uses the same trust-region Newton driver on the remaining coordinates, with the scales concentrated out. The theory and the chi-bar-square weights are in the population inference vignette.

The L-BFGS-B branch of deconvolute_single_cell() can return an exact zero. There the ILR coordinates, the Wald covariances and the Wald and ILR intervals are undefined (NA); the profile interval and the boundary test are the procedures that remain valid.

What these intervals do not cover

  • The reference is a plug-in. Every method except the reference bootstrap treats (\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}) as known. No sandwich or higher-order term corrects for the estimation of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j}; the reference bootstrap is the implemented route.
  • One donor has no between-donor layer. \phi inflates the covariance globally but cannot correct its shape, so with a reference from one donor the intervals describe within-donor variation only.
  • The variance function must be right. The determinant term of the likelihood adds information only if \phi\,\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}) is the true covariance. Otherwise the quasi-score of the generalised linear model view is the safer estimator.
  • Gaussian cells. The sum of Gaussian cells is exactly Gaussian. For count data, Eq. 7 is a central-limit approximation that needs many cells of every type.
